chapter: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
title: Boogie Woogie on St. Louis Blues and the 1940 dates

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: I see. I see. There's a story that Art Tatum was so taken with "Japanese Sandman" that -- and Wallace Bishop's playing, that when he first met Wallace he called him, Mr. Sandman. That was an awfully good record. Speaking of arrangements, or routines that came about, how did "Boogie Woogie on St. Louis Blues" come about?
I think that was mostly head.
Yeah, it sounds like a head.
Mostly head. Earl got the idea to start out with the Boogie. I guess he just decided to go with the Boogie.
Yeah, boogie woogie had come back into popularity about that time. When was that recorded, about '39?
Yeah.
Or '40. Somewhere in there.
Thirties. Must have been '39, because it's just before I left the band.
Yeah. Well, I wanted to ask you about that. There's some dates from 1940 that according to this you're on. Recorded February 13th, 1940, in New York City, and June 19th, 1940.
Yeah. Well, that would be right.
Well, you left the band in the last part of 1940?
Last part, yeah. Last part of '40.
I see. But that '39, '40 band is an awful good band.
Yeah.
That was an excellent, excellent band. Really tight, and everything swung. Swung hard, too. You know, one of these records has an alternate take of "St. Louis Blues," but there's no yelling on it.
Uh-huh.

And it really -- you know, I'm waiting for it. I played it last night, and didn't realize I was playing the one that wasn't issued at the time. I said, 'I dolgarn know that there's some shouts on there.' George Dixon did those shouts?
He did the shouts.
And it really is an odd sensation to hear that after years of hearing the other one. Because it's --
It goes -- it all goes together.
Right. Well, did he -- well, it was recorded two different ways. Did he start the shouting in the studio, or did he start that on the job?
He started that in the studio.
When he recorded it.

When we recorded it. And it sounded so good to him, Earl's solos, you know, He'd shout out different things. And when he said, 'Play it until 1951,' man, everybody started to figure, hey, are we going to be here that long? Oh, that was a long way off.
I guess that's easily the best known Earl Hines record.
Yeah.
And I think maybe the shouting had a lot to do with --
Had a lot to do with it. Had a lot to do with it.
I still hear guys do things like that, you know.
(Unintelligible) right now.
Right, right. Play it until 1991, or something.
Yeah, but I mean they do now.
Yeah, 1991.
That was probably George Dixon's greatest influence.
Yes.
(Laughter.)
